Box-Jenkins Forecasting: SARIMA Modeling of Pharmaceutical Sales

Evaluating Seasonal Demand and Model Ensembles for Antihistamine Sales (R06)

1 Introduction & Problem Framing

This project applies the Box-Jenkins methodology to analyze and forecast the sales volume of pharmaceutical products, specifically focusing on the R06 category (Antihistamines for systemic use).
The dataset consists of Pharmacy Point-of-Sale transactions, which have been aggregated to a monthly frequency.

Because antihistamine demand is heavily driven by real-world biological cycles, this series is expected to exhibit strong, predictable seasonal fluctuations.

Accurate forecasting on this localized scale holds significant business value for individual pharmacies. It allows them to anticipate peak demand, optimize inventory procurement, and prevent stock-outs.

By validating a parsimonious ARIMA model, this analysis aims to determine whether short-term antihistamine demand can be reliably predicted using only its own historical autoregressive and seasonal memory.

2 Exploratory Data Analysis & Preprocessing

2.1 Visual Inspection and STL Decomposition

Visual inspection of the raw antihistamine sales reveals a clear 12-month seasonal pattern. Furthermore, the amplitude of the seasonal fluctuations is not constant; the variance appears to increase with the level of the series. Because the variance is non-constant, a variance stabilization transformation is formally required before proceeding to stationarity tests.

2.2 Variance Stabilization Evaluation

Variance Stabilization Diagnostic (Training Set)
Method Optimal_Lambda Transformation
Guerrero Optimization -0.312 Box-Cox Required

During our initial visual inspection, the amplitude of the seasonal sales fluctuations appeared to increase alongside the overall level of the series, suggesting non-constant variance. To formally test this, we applied the Guerrero method to the training data. The calculation yielded an optimal Box-Cox parameter (λ) of -0.312, which is significantly distinct of 1.0.

This mathematical result confirms our visual hypothesis: the variance is non-constant. Therefore, the Box-Cox transformation is strictly required to stabilize the variance across the series, satisfying the prerequisite assumptions for formal Box-Jenkins estimation.

2.3 Stationarity Diagnostics and Differencing

ADF Unit Root Diagnostics (GTS Procedure). T-test for zero mean on differenced series: p = 0.4239
Data_State ADF_Type Optimal_Lags Test_Statistic Critical_5pct Conclusion
Box-Cox Transformed trend 11 -1.0734 -3.45 Non-Stationary
Box-Cox + Seasonal Diff (D=1) none 12 -1.2193 -1.95 Stationary

Stationarity was evaluated on the Box-Cox transformed series using the ADF test via the GTS lag reduction procedure (initialized at 16 lags). The transformed level data failed to reject the unit root null under a trend specification, confirming non-stationarity. A seasonal difference (D=1) was applied, and a formal t-test confirmed the differenced series has a mean not significantly different from zero (p > 0.05), justifying the switch to type=“none”. Retesting under GTS confirmed the differenced series rejects the unit root null at the 5% level. No regular differencing was required (d=0). The series is now fully stationary with integration orders d=0, D=1.

Visual inspection of the correlograms reveals significant spikes at early non-seasonal lags (lag 1 and 3), indicating regular autoregressive or moving average memory (p=1p=1 or q=1q=1). At the seasonal lags, significant activity at lags 12 and 24 confirms the need for seasonal parameters (P=1P=1 and/or Q=1Q=1). Because we achieved stationarity without regular differencing (d=0d=0) but required a seasonal difference (D=1D=1), our candidates follow a general SARIMA(p,0,q)(P,1,Q)12(p,0,q)(P,1,Q)12 structure. We estimated seven manual permutations derived from these diagnostics alongside an automated benchmark. The models are ranked by the Corrected Akaike Information Criterion (AICc) to identify the optimal balance between goodness-of-fit and parameter parsimony.

With the optimal specification confirmed by report() above, we proceed to residual validation.

4 Residual Diagnostics

To validate the model for forecasting, we must ensure its residuals are consistent with white noise. We analyze the residual Autocorrelation Function (ACF) visually and formally test for remaining serial dependence using the Ljung-Box test.

## 
## 
## Table: Ljung-Box test (lag=24) with model-specific degrees of freedom
## 
## |    Model     | DoF | Ljung-Box stat | p-value |
## |:------------:|:---:|:--------------:|:-------:|
## | sarima000110 |  2  |    53.7653     | 0.0002  |
## | sarima001110 |  3  |    48.9129     | 0.0005  |
## | sarima100110 |  3  |    46.2774     | 0.0012  |
## | sarima000011 |  1  |    47.2358     | 0.0021  |
## | sarima000111 |  2  |    45.4349     | 0.0023  |
## | sarima200110 |  3  |    34.9989     | 0.0282  |
## | sarima001011 |  2  |    36.0004     | 0.0304  |
## | sarima001111 |  3  |    34.6999     | 0.0305  |
## | sarima101011 |  3  |    23.9776     | 0.2941  |

To rigorously validate our candidate pool, we applied the formal Ljung-Box test (lag=24lag=24) to the residuals of all estimated models. Candidate specifications that violated invertibility constraints and failed Maximum Likelihood Estimation were excluded from the diagnostic pool. For the remaining viable models, the null hypothesis states that the residuals are independent white noise. Visual inspection of the optimal sarima(101011) specification’s residuals confirms homoskedastic variance, and its Ljung-Box p-value safely exceeds 0.05, mathematically proving an absence of significant autocorrelation and corroborating its validity for forecasting.

In both evaluations, we sorted the values by RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and MASE, and we even compared the in-sample values with the out-of-sample ones. In fact, our two best ‘out-of-sample’ are the models that passed the Ljung-Box test.

In order to create a single forecast chart, we combined the models that passed the Ljung-Box test, where the lower the RMSE of the selected models, the more weight they carry in the final combined model.

In fact, the RMSE of the combined model is higher than that of all the individual models, meaning we achieved a worse model through this combination, so the best idea is to take a step back and stop with the best-performing model, Sarima101011.

6.2 Out-of-Sample Forecast Evaluation

Out-of-Sample Forecast Accuracy (16-Month Holdout)
.model RMSE MAE MAPE MASE
ETS 0.0678 0.0576 2.3812 0.9805
sarima101011 0.0690 0.0583 2.4121 0.9931
Seasonal_Naive 0.0965 0.0826 3.3914 1.4059
Historical_Mean 0.1274 0.1136 4.6388 1.9345

Auto ARIMA, ETS, Seasonal Naïve, and Historical Mean were evaluated on a 16-month test set using standard error metrics (RMSE, MAE, MAPE, MASE). ETS marginally outperformed SARIMA on RMSE. This reflects a small-sample effect: with only 53 training observations, SARIMA’s extra parameters introduce estimation variance that simpler methods avoid. However, SARIMA remains practically advantageous, providing structurally interpretable coefficients that explicitly identify the seasonal mechanisms driving demand

7 Conclusion, Limitations & Reflections

7.1 Summary of Findings

This study applied the Box-Jenkins methodology to monthly antihistamine sales at a Portuguese pharmacy. Stationarity was achieved using a Box-Cox transformation (λ ≈ -0.312) and one seasonal difference (D=1). The optimal model, SARIMA(1,0,1)(0,1,1)₁₂, was validated by white-noise residuals (Ljung-Box p > 0.05). Structurally, the seasonal MA(1) captures annual allergy cycles, while the regular ARMA(1,1) reflects month-to-month purchasing delays. Although ETS slightly outperformed SARIMA on RMSE during a 16-month holdout—a known small-sample effect given the 53 training observations—SARIMA remains the preferred model for its superior interpretability.

7.2 Limitations

The main constraint is sample size. With approximately 69 monthly observations total, parameter estimates carry substantial uncertainty and out-of-sample comparisons are sensitive to the chosen holdout window. A longer record ideally ten or more years would improve model stability considerably.

The dataset also covers a single pharmacy location, limiting generalizability. Regional pollen calendars, local demographics, and prescribing patterns all affect antihistamine demand and are invisible to a univariate ARIMA framework. A dataset with genuine seasonal structure was deliberately chosen to showcase the full Box-Jenkins workflow; a multivariate ARIMAX extension incorporating pollen count indices or temperature data as exogenous regressors would likely improve both fit and forecasting precision.

7.3 Future Research

A natural extension would apply the same framework to other drug categories in the dataset (e.g. N02 analgesics or C10 cardiovascular agents) to assess whether seasonal patterns generalize across therapeutic classes. Forecast combination — weighting SARIMA, ETS, and SNAIVE by inverse training RMSE — could further improve out-of-sample precision beyond any single specification, as demonstrated in Timmermann (2006).
